topic: Quality layer for satishregonda.in — performance budget, WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility, SEO/JSON-LD, Google Scholar (Highwire) indexing, scientific dark mode, print/CV, longevity, and India DPDP/privacy — with verified thresholds, official quotes and shippable code.
key_findings: Google Scholar's own guidance for THIS exact case (verbatim, fetched from scholar.google.com/intl/en/scholar/inclusion.html): 'If you're an individual author, it works best to simply upload your paper to your website, e.g., www.example.edu/~professor/jpdr2009.pdf; and add a link to it on your publications page... Make sure that: the full text of your paper is in a PDF file that ends with ".pdf", the title of the paper appears in a large font on top of the first page, the authors of the paper are listed right below the title on a separate line, and there's a bibliography section titled, e.g., "References"... Our search robots should normally find your paper and include it in Google Scholar within several weeks.'

HARD, NON-OBVIOUS SCHOLAR CONSTRAINT: 'The content of the tag is the absolute URL of the PDF file; for security reasons, it must refer to a file in the same subdirectory as the HTML abstract.' This dictates URL architecture: /publications/2024-musi-urban-flood/index.html + /publications/2024-musi-urban-flood/paper.pdf. A central /pdfs/ folder BREAKS citation_pdf_url.

SCHOLAR KILLS THE OBVIOUS DESIGN: 'Your website must not require users (or search robots) to sign in, install special software, accept disclaimers, dismiss popup or interstitial advertisements, click on links or buttons, or scroll down the page before they can read the entire abstract of the paper.' A click-to-expand accordion abstract on the per-paper page is a Scholar disqualifier. Also: 'the use of Flash, JavaScript, or form-based navigation makes it hard for our automated system to find your articles.' → the Google-Sheets pipeline MUST be build-time, never a client-side fetch.

Scholar also requires: one paper = one URL ('we're unable to effectively index multiple abstracts on the same webpage'); PDFs must have searchable text; each file ≤5MB; minimum viable meta set is exactly three fields — title, at least the first author's full name, and year — and 'Pages that don't provide any one of these three fields will be processed as if they had no meta tags at all.' Timing: new papers added 'several times a week', but updates to already-indexed papers 'usually take 6-9 months'.

Verified Highwire tags in the wild via raw curl: arXiv (arxiv.org/abs/2401.00001) emits citation_title, repeated citation_author in 'Surname, Given' form, citation_date as 2023/11/18, citation_pdf_url, citation_abstract. HESS/Copernicus (hess.copernicus.org/articles/28/1/2024/) adds citation_publisher, citation_journal_title, citation_volume, citation_issue, citation_issn, citation_doi, citation_firstpage, citation_lastpage, citation_author_institution, citation_author_orcid, citation_fulltext_world_readable. Scholar's own date format spec: 'Provide full dates in the "2010/5/12" format if available; or a year alone otherwise.'

Google's structured-data rich-results gallery does NOT list Person or ScholarlyArticle as supported rich-result types. ProfilePage IS supported and is the correct wrapper: mainEntity (Person|Organization) and name are REQUIRED; dateCreated, dateModified, alternateName, description, image, sameAs are recommended. Article/BlogPosting and Course list are supported; Organization is supported.

HTTP Archive 2024 page-weight medians to beat: mobile total 1,938 KB (desktop 2,157 KB); mobile JS 570 KB; mobile images 900 KB; mobile CSS 75 KB; mobile fonts 111 KB. 10th percentile mobile total is 471 KB. A 150–250 KB first view puts this site below the 10th percentile — i.e. faster than 90% of the web.

Core Web Vitals thresholds (web.dev/articles/vitals), all measured at the 75th percentile segmented by mobile/desktop: LCP ≤2.5s, INP ≤200ms, CLS ≤0.1. FID was retired in 2024. LCP sub-part budget from web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp: TTFB ~40%, resource load delay <10%, resource load duration ~40%, element render delay <10%. 'Never lazy-load your LCP image.'

font-display exact periods (CSS Fonts 4 §4.9 + web.dev): block = 0–3s block / infinite swap; swap = 0ms block / infinite swap; fallback = 100ms block / 3s swap; optional = 100ms block / 0ms swap. MDN's page wrongly claims swap is 'best for CLS' — it is the WORST for CLS (infinite swap window = a guaranteed reflow whenever the font arrives late). `optional` is the only zero-CLS choice.

Dan Luu's measured load times on real slow links (danluu.com/web-bloat/): his ~0.01–0.1 MB text site loaded in 1.6s on dial-up and 6.4s on a 'bad' connection (dial-up bandwidth + 1000ms ping + 10% packet loss), while google.com took 94s on dial-up / 6.8s on 3G and amazon.com 265s / 36s. joelonsoftware.com FAILED entirely (6-minute timeout). Page weight, not cleverness, is what survives Indian 3G.

WCAG 2.2 conformance levels verified against the normative W3C spec (many blog posts get these wrong): 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) = AA; 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) = AAA; 2.4.13 Focus Appearance = AAA; 2.5.7 Dragging Movements = AA; 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) = AA (24×24 CSS px); 3.2.6 Consistent Help = A; 3.3.7 Redundant Entry = A; 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) = AA. Contrast: 4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text (≥18pt or ≥14pt bold), 3:1 non-text/UI/graphical objects (1.4.11).

WebAIM Screen Reader Survey #10: 71.6% of screen-reader users navigate a long page by HEADINGS first (78% of advanced users), vs 13.6% find-in-page, 4.8% links, 3.7% landmarks. 88.8% rate heading levels useful. Top-10 problem list includes 'Unclear link/button text' at #3 and 'Images with missing or improper descriptions (alt text)' at #6 — exactly the two things a publications list gets wrong (forty links all labelled 'PDF', and undescribed hydrographs).

Dark-mode figures: gwern.net/design solves this with per-image ML classification via InvertOrNot.com — a real, fetched API (POST https://invertornot.com/api/url with a JSON array of URLs → [{invert:0|1, sha1, error, url}]; also /api/file and /api/sha1, accepting JPG/PNG/WebP/SVG/PDF). Run it at BUILD time to tag which figures may be inverted. Blanket `filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg)` is wrong: it negates headshots and reverses the semantics of diverging colormaps and flood-depth ramps.

MathML Core is Baseline 'widely available' since January 2023 and renders equations natively with zero JavaScript, inheriting currentColor so dark mode 'just works' — versus KaTeX/MathJax which ship hundreds of KB of fonts and cause font-swap CLS. Pre-render LaTeX→MathML at build time.

<picture> supports media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" on <source> (verified on MDN) — the honest solution for raster maps and satellite imagery that cannot be re-rendered: ship two exports rather than inverting one.

Image format facts (MDN): AVIF is ~50% smaller than JPEG at similar quality, WebP ~25–35% smaller than JPEG and ~26% smaller than lossless PNG. BUT 'AVIF does not support progressive rendering—files must fully download before display', which matters on 3G. MDN's explicit recommendation for 'Diagrams, drawings, charts' is SVG, fallback PNG — so hydrographs and schematics should ship as optimised SVG, not raster.

Cookieless analytics, verified: Plausible's script is 2.5 KB gzipped vs GA4's 135 KB, uses no cookies and 'generate[s] a random string of letters and numbers to calculate unique visitors on a given day and reset[s] this string daily' — no consent banner claimed necessary. GoatCounter stores only aggregate data and says it 'probably doesn't require a GDPR consent notice'. Cloudflare Web Analytics is free 'on all plans' and privacy-first.

India's DPDP Act 2023 applies to digital personal data collected in India and to processing outside India where goods/services are offered in India. Consent must be preceded by a notice stating what is collected and why; consent is withdrawable; there are Data Fiduciary obligations (accuracy, safeguards, breach reporting to the Data Protection Board, erasure once purpose is met) and Schedule penalties up to ₹250 crore for security failures. Research/archiving/statistical purposes are exempted.

Verified from this machine (curl to cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace): loc=IN, colo=DEL — Cloudflare terminates at its Delhi PoP for Indian traffic, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3. Cloudflare Pages therefore gives Indian readers sub-100ms TTFB from an Indian edge.

Current state, verified: satishregonda.in and raftwaters.in have NO DNS A or NS records yet (dig returned empty for both) — nothing is live. The existing Google Site returns a 135,178-byte HTML shell before any CSS/JS/images. IITH lists him as 'Satish Kumar Regonda', Associate Professor, Civil Engineering + Climate Change, satishr@ce.iith.ac.in; the Google Site brands him 'Satish Regonda' — a name-variant split that must be resolved for entity SEO.

Lighthouse budget.json (GoogleChrome/budget.json) supports resourceSizes/resourceCounts for exactly these resourceTypes: document, font, image, media, other, script, stylesheet, third-party, total — and accepts per-path budgets, so /publications/* can carry a different budget from /notes/*.
recommendations: ADOPT THIS PERFORMANCE BUDGET and enforce it in CI with Lighthouse budget.json: total ≤175 KB first view (homepage), ≤250 KB on a figure-heavy publication page; HTML ≤15 KB gz; CSS ≤14 KB gz inlined (fits the ~14 KB initial TCP congestion window, so first paint costs one RTT); JS ≤20 KB gz shipped and ≤10 KB executed on load, with ZERO JS required to read any content; fonts ≤60 KB total (2 subset WOFF2 files); LCP image ≤80 KB AVIF. Internal targets stricter than Google's: LCP ≤1.5s, INP ≤100ms, CLS ≤0.02, TTFB ≤400ms — measured on Lighthouse Slow 4G, not on your laptop.

MAKE THE GOOGLE SHEETS PIPELINE BUILD-TIME AND SELF-ARCHIVING. Fetch the Sheets/Docs at build, then COMMIT the fetched JSON/CSV back into the repo before generating pages. This single decision solves three problems at once: (a) Scholar's crawler can't run JS, so client-side Sheet fetching would make publications invisible to Scholar and to Google; (b) it keeps runtime JS at zero; (c) in ten years, if the Sheet is deleted or the API changes, the repo alone still rebuilds the site byte-for-byte. Trigger rebuilds from a Sheets 'Publish' button (Apps Script → deploy webhook) plus a nightly cron.

URL ARCHITECTURE, frozen on day one: /publications/<year>-<slug>/ with the PDF as a SIBLING file inside that same directory (/publications/2024-musi-urban-flood/paper.pdf) because Scholar requires citation_pdf_url to point into the same subdirectory as the HTML abstract. Blog at /notes/<slug>/ (no dates in the path — he will backdate). RAFT at /raft/. CV at /cv/ (HTML) plus /cv.pdf (a permanent 302 to the current dated file /cv/regonda-cv-2026-09.pdf). Never encode venue, Sheet row id, or issue number in a slug. Trailing slash always; 301 the non-slash and the www form.

GIVE EVERY PUBLICATION ITS OWN HTML ABSTRACT PAGE with the full author-written abstract visible in the initial HTML — no accordion, no 'read abstract' button, no JS. Add the Highwire meta set + a self-referencing canonical + ScholarlyArticle JSON-LD. Belt-and-braces the PDF too: title in ≥24pt at the top of page one, authors on the next line at 16–23pt, a 'References' heading, Type 1 fonts from LaTeX (\usepackage{times}). Check publisher self-archiving rights per paper (accepted manuscript vs version of record) before posting any PDF.

SELF-HOST TWO SUBSET WOFF2 FILES. Never fonts.googleapis.com: it is a render-blocking stylesheet on a third origin costing ~3 extra RTTs (≈450ms at India's 150ms RTT), it hands the reader's IP to Google (a DPDP/GDPR liability for zero benefit), and browser HTTP cache is now partitioned per-site so the old 'shared cache' argument is dead. Subset with pyftsubset to Latin + Latin-1 + the scientific glyphs he actually uses (³ ° − × ≈ ≤ ≥ ± μ σ Δ ∼ – — ' ' " " …). Preload ONLY the regular weight, with crossorigin (mandatory even same-origin or the browser fetches it twice). font-display: swap plus a metric-matched local() fallback with size-adjust/ascent-override to neutralise the swap reflow.

SHIP HYDROGRAPHS AND SCHEMATICS AS SVG, NOT PNG. Export from R/ggplot or matplotlib with a transparent background, run through svgo, inline it, and set axes/ticks/labels to `stroke: currentColor; fill: currentColor` — the figure then follows light/dark automatically, stays sharp on every DPI, is text-selectable, and typically weighs 15–40 KB. Reserve raster (AVIF+WebP+JPEG via <picture>) for maps with basemaps, satellite/drone imagery and model-output rasters, and give those a dual dark export via <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">.

NEVER blanket-invert images in dark mode. Default to no filter. Wrap unconvertible white-background figures in a light 'plate' (white/near-white card with padding and a 1px border) that sits inside the dark page — this is the honest, legible answer and it is what a printed journal figure looks like anyway. If you want per-image inversion for pure line art, run InvertOrNot's /api/url at build time and emit a data-invert attribute; do it at build, never at runtime.

USE MathML CORE FOR EQUATIONS, pre-rendered at build (pandoc or KaTeX's mathml output). Zero runtime JS, zero font-swap CLS, inherits currentColor so dark mode works for free, and it lands in the accessibility tree for screen readers. Drop KaTeX/MathJax entirely.

FIX THE THREE ACCESSIBILITY FAILURES THAT DEFINE ACADEMIC SITES: (1) light-grey metadata — #999 on white is 2.85:1 and FAILS; use #595959 (7:1) for muted text and #767676 (4.54:1) as the absolute floor; (2) forty links labelled 'PDF' — append a visually-hidden qualifier ('PDF — Regonda et al. 2024, Urban flood forecasting for Hyderabad'); (3) undescribed figures — alt says what it IS, figcaption says what it MEANS, and a
data table gives the numbers.

ALT TEXT CONVENTION FOR THIS SITE, write it into the Sheet as a required column: hydrograph → alt="Line chart of observed and forecast discharge at the Musi River, Hyderabad, 1–15 October 2020." with the finding in the caption ('Observed discharge peaked at 1,240 m³/s on 14 October, ~30% above the ensemble median; the 90% band captured the peak.'). Map → alt="Map of Hyderabad showing modelled inundation depth for the October 2020 event." plus a caption that translates the colour ramp into words and names the spatial pattern. Headshot adjacent to his name in text → alt="" (W3C decision tree: content redundant to nearby text takes an empty alt). Decorative texture → CSS background, never an .

BUILD THE PUBLICATIONS FILTER AS PROGRESSIVE ENHANCEMENT. Server-render the complete list; layer filtering on top with real <button aria-pressed> or checkboxes inside <fieldset><legend>, announce the count in aria-live="polite" ('18 publications match'), and keep filter state in the URL query so results are linkable and the back button works. This satisfies keyboard access, satisfies Scholar's 'no JavaScript navigation' rule, and works on a dead 3G connection. If you can do it with CSS :has() + checkboxes, ship 0 KB of JS.

PUT A ProfilePage/@graph JSON-LD BLOCK ON THE HOMEPAGE with @id anchors so the Person node is defined once and referenced from every other page. sameAs must list Google Scholar, ORCID, ResearchGate, LinkedIn, the IITH faculty page and raftwaters.in. Resolve the name split: pick 'Satish Regonda' as `name` (matches the domain) and put 'Satish Kumar Regonda', 'S. K. Regonda' and 'Regonda, Satish' in alternateName. Then add satishregonda.in to the Homepage field of his Scholar profile, ORCID, ResearchGate, LinkedIn and the IITH CMS — those inbound links from high-authority domains are what actually wins the name query.

GENERATE PER-PAGE OG IMAGES AT BUILD TIME with Satori → resvg/sharp at 1200×630 (1.91:1, ≤8 MB per Facebook's spec). Publication cards get title + author list + venue + year; notes get the title + date; the homepage gets name + role + institution. Keep an UNSUBSETTED TTF/OTF of the display face in the repo for this — Satori accepts TTF/OTF/WOFF but NOT WOFF2. Always set og:image:alt. A single site-wide OG image is the clearest tell of a templated site.

SHIP A REAL PRINT STYLESHEET AND FORCE LIGHT WHEN PRINTING. A dark-mode site printed as-is comes out black-on-black, because browsers drop background colours by default while keeping text colours. @media print must reset color-scheme: light, background #fff, colour #000; hide nav/footer/theme toggle/skip link; use @page { size: A4; margin: 18mm 16mm } (A4, not Letter — this is India); break-inside: avoid on figure, .cv-entry and each publication; break-after: avoid on h2/h3; orphans/widows: 3. Expand link URLs only inside prose (.prose a[href^="http"]::after), never inside the publication list or the printout becomes unreadable.

MAKE THE CV DUAL-FORMAT FROM ONE SOURCE. /cv/ is semantic HTML generated from the same Sheets data (indexable, accessible, always current); the PDF is generated at build from that same HTML via WeasyPrint or Paged.js so the two can never drift, published at a dated path with a stable /cv.pdf alias. This also means he updates his CV by editing a Sheet, which is the whole point of the project.

ANALYTICS: prefer server-side log analysis (GoAccess over Cloudflare logs) = 0 KB of client JS and zero personal data leaving the edge. If he needs a dashboard he'll actually look at, Plausible (2.5 KB, no cookies, daily-rotating identifier) or Cloudflare Web Analytics (free, already on the edge you're using). Never GA4 — 135 KB, cookies, a consent banner, and a third-party data transfer you'd have to write a DPDP notice for.

COLLECT NOTHING and you have almost no DPDP surface: no contact form (plain mailto), no newsletter (RSS instead), no comments (email instead), no embedded YouTube/Twitter (click-to-load facade or a plain link — embeds are third-party trackers). If a form is ever added, put a one-paragraph notice at the point of collection saying what is collected, why, and how to withdraw, per the Act's notice-before-consent requirement, and add a /privacy/ page.

EMAIL: publish satishr@ce.iith.ac.in as a plain, copy-pasteable mailto link, optionally with @ and . as HTML entities (@, .) — that is the ONE obfuscation with zero accessibility or usability cost. Do NOT use the current site's 'satishr.at.iith.ac.in' text form, CSS direction:rtl reversal (screen readers read it backwards), JS assembly (breaks without JS), or an image (a hard WCAG failure). His address is already in plain text on the IITH faculty page, so obfuscation on this site buys nothing.

LINK-ROT PROGRAMME: cite DOIs (https://doi.org/…) not publisher landing pages; cite Zenodo DOIs not GitHub URLs for code/data; run lychee or linkchecker in CI on every build and fail on 404s; at build time query the Wayback Availability API (https://archive.org/wayback/available?url=…) for every external link in a blog post and emit a small [archived] companion link; POST the sitemap URLs to Save Page Now on each deploy so the site itself is preserved. Keep an append-only _redirects file — a slug, once published, is never deleted, only redirected.

SET THE TEN-YEAR FLOOR: no build-time dependency that can silently die (Sheets data committed to the repo; fonts vendored; no CDN-loaded JS libraries); a mirror deploy to GitHub Pages as a cold standby on a *.github.io URL; the domain registered for the maximum term with auto-renew and a second contact email; the whole repo public so a student or successor can rebuild it. Add security headers on the static host: HSTS max-age=63072000 includeSubDomains preload, a tight CSP (trivial when you self-host everything), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=().

## 1. Performance budget ### Verified benchmarks to beat (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024, page-weight chapter) | Percentile | Total (mobile) | Total (desktop) | |---|---|---| | 10th | 471 KB | 549 KB | | 25th | 995 KB | 1,138 KB | | **50th** | **1,938 KB** | **2,157 KB** | | 75th | 3,766 KB | 4,169 KB | | 90th | 7,680 KB | 8,375 KB | Median mobile by type: **JS 570 KB, images 900 KB, CSS 75 KB, fonts 111 KB**. Mobile JS at the 10th percentile is still 89 KB. ### The budget for this site | Resource | Homepage | Publication page | Note page | |---|---|---|---| | HTML (gz) | ≤ 15 KB | ≤ 20 KB | ≤ 25 KB | | CSS (gz, inlined) | ≤ 14 KB | ≤ 14 KB | ≤ 14 KB | | JS (gz, shipped) | ≤ 20 KB | ≤ 20 KB | ≤ 20 KB | | JS executed on load | ≤ 10 KB | ≤ 10 KB | ≤ 10 KB | | Fonts | ≤ 60 KB | ≤ 60 KB | ≤ 60 KB | | Images (first view) | ≤ 80 KB | ≤ 140 KB | ≤ 120 KB | | **Total first view** | **≤ 175 KB** | **≤ 250 KB** | **≤ 230 KB** | The 14 KB CSS number is deliberate: TCP slow start delivers ~10 segments × ~1460 B ≈ 14.6 KB in the first round trip, so a critical CSS payload under that renders in one RTT. *(Widely-cited networking figure; not re-verified in this session.)* ### Core Web Vitals (web.dev/articles/vitals — all at **p75**, segmented mobile/desktop) - **LCP ≤ 2.5 s** (good) · **INP ≤ 200 ms** · **CLS ≤ 0.1** - FID was retired in 2024, replaced by INP. **Internal targets (stricter, so field data has headroom):** LCP ≤ 1.5 s, INP ≤ 100 ms, CLS ≤ 0.02, TTFB ≤ 400 ms. ### LCP sub-budget (web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp) | Sub-part | Budget | |---|---| | TTFB | ~40% | | Resource load delay | < 10% | | Resource load duration | ~40% | | Element render delay | < 10% | Against a 1.5 s target: TTFB ≤ 600 ms, load delay ≤ 150 ms, load duration ≤ 600 ms, render delay ≤ 150 ms. Two rules quoted directly: **"Never lazy-load your LCP image"**, and use `fetchpriority="high"` plus discoverability from the initial HTML. ### The 3G-in-India reality check Dan Luu's measurements (danluu.com/web-bloat/) of real slow links: | Site | Dial-up | 3G | "Bad" (dial-up BW, 1000 ms ping, 10% loss) | |---|---|---|---| | danluu.com (~0.01–0.1 MB) | 1.6 s | — | 6.4 s | | google.com (0.59 MB) | 94 s | 6.8 s | 96 s | | reddit.com | — | 20 s | — | | amazon.com (4.4 MB) | 265 s | 36 s | 300 s | | joelonsoftware.com | — | — | **FAIL (6 min timeout)** | Arithmetic for the budget: on Lighthouse Slow 4G (~1.6 Mbit/s, 150 ms RTT) a 175 KB page transfers in ~0.9 s; add ~4 RTTs of DNS+TCP+TLS+HTML ≈ 0.6 s cold → ~1.5 s LCP. On real 3G at ~400 kbit/s the same page is ~3.5 s. At the HTTP Archive median of 1,938 KB it would be ~40 s. **Page weight is the whole game.** ### Hosting — verified from this machine ``` $ curl -s https://www.cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace loc=IN colo=DEL ← Cloudflare Delhi PoP http=http/2 tls=TLSv1.3 ``` Cloudflare Pages therefore serves Indian readers from an Indian edge. Prefer it over Netlify/Vercel for this audience. *(Comparative India PoP coverage for Netlify/Vercel: UNVERIFIED.)* ### Current-state baseline ``` $ curl -o /dev/null -w "%{size_download}" https://sites.google.com/iith.ac.in/satishregonda/home 135178 ← 135 KB of HTML shell, before any CSS/JS/images ``` The new homepage should ship *the entire page* in roughly that budget. ``` $ dig +short satishregonda.in A ; dig +short raftwaters.in A (empty) ← neither domain resolves yet ``` ### Fonts **Exact `font-display` periods** (CSS Fonts 4 §4.9, cross-checked with web.dev): | Value | Block period | Swap period | |---|---|---| | `block` | 0–3 s | infinite | | `swap` | 0 ms | infinite | | `fallback` | 100 ms | 3 s | | `optional` | 100 ms | **0 ms** | > ⚠️ MDN's `font-display` page states "`swap` is generally best for CLS". **That is wrong.** An infinite swap period guarantees a reflow whenever the font arrives late. `optional` is the only value that cannot cause a font-swap layout shift. Choose `swap` + metric-matched fallback if the typeface *is* the design (which it is here); choose `optional` if you want CLS ≡ 0 and accept that some first-time 3G visitors see the fallback. ```html ``` `crossorigin` is **mandatory even same-origin** — without it the browser fetches the file twice. ```css @font-face{ font-family:"Site Serif"; src:url("/f/serif-400.woff2") format("woff2"); font-weight:400; font-style:normal; font-display:swap; } /* metric-matched fallback kills the swap reflow — MEASURE these per pairing with the Fallback Font Generator; the numbers below are illustrative */ @font-face{ font-family:"Site Serif Fallback"; src:local("Georgia"),local("Times New Roman"),local("Nimbus Roman"); size-adjust:105%; ascent-override:95%; descent-override:25%; line-gap-override:0%; } body{ font-family:"Site Serif","Site Serif Fallback",Georgia,serif; } /* publication years, table columns, data */ .pub-year, table td { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; } ``` Subsetting: ```bash pyftsubset SourceSerif4-Regular.ttf \ --output-file=serif-400.woff2 --flavor=woff2 --layout-features='*' \ --unicodes='U+0000-00FF,U+0131,U+0152-0153,U+02BB-02BC,U+2000-206F,U+2074,U+20B9,\ U+2122,U+2212,U+2215,U+00B0,U+00B1,U+00B3,U+00D7,U+2248,U+2264,U+2265,U+03BC,U+03C3,U+0394,U+223C' ``` (₹ = U+20B9 is worth keeping for an Indian site.) A subset text face lands ~18–30 KB per weight in WOFF2. Two static weights beat a variable font on bytes unless you need ≥3 weights. Italic needs its own file — synthetic oblique on a serif looks broken. `unicode-range` splitting is **not** worth it for a Latin-only site. It becomes essential the moment he adds Telugu: ```css @font-face{ font-family:"Site Telugu"; src:url("/f/telugu.woff2") format("woff2"); unicode-range:U+0C00-0C7F; font-display:swap; } ``` **Do not use fonts.googleapis.com.** It costs a render-blocking stylesheet on a third origin (~3 extra RTTs ≈ 450 ms at 150 ms RTT), sends the reader's IP to Google (a DPDP notice obligation for zero benefit), and browser HTTP cache is now partitioned per-site, so the historical "shared cache" argument no longer exists. ### Images MDN facts: **AVIF ≈ 50% smaller than JPEG**; **WebP ≈ 25–35% smaller than JPEG, ≈ 26% smaller than lossless PNG**. But: *"AVIF does not support progressive rendering—files must fully download before display"* — relevant on 3G for a large hero. MDN's recommendation for **"Diagrams, drawings, charts"** is **SVG**, fallback PNG. ```html ``` - `width`/`height` attributes → browser derives `aspect-ratio` → **zero CLS**. Add `style="aspect-ratio:16/9"` when CSS resizes it. - `loading="lazy" decoding="async"` below the fold; **never on the LCP element**, which instead gets `fetchpriority="high"`. - web.dev: *"It's common to serve 3-5 different sizes of an image."* For a 720 px content column: 720/1080/1440. - **LQIP:** skip blur-up. A flat average-colour background costs ~20 bytes and no decode; a 20×20 blurred data-URI costs 300–600 bytes plus a decode. On a text-heavy site nobody misses the blur. - Strip EXIF from field/drone photos — GPS coordinates in a flood-survey photo are a privacy problem (`exiftool -all= *.jpg`, or sharp strips by default). ### Long pages ```css .pub-year-group, .note-section { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 600px; /* REQUIRED, or you get scrollbar jitter/CLS */ } ``` `content-visibility: auto` keeps content in the a11y tree, find-in-page and tab order (unlike `hidden`). Baseline since Sept 2024. ### CI enforcement — `budget.json` Supported `resourceType` values (GoogleChrome/budget.json): `document, font, image, media, other, script, stylesheet, third-party, total`. ```json [ { "path": "/*", "resourceSizes": [ { "resourceType": "total", "budget": 175 }, { "resourceType": "script", "budget": 20 }, { "resourceType": "stylesheet", "budget": 14 }, { "resourceType": "font", "budget": 60 }, { "resourceType": "image", "budget": 80 } ], "resourceCounts": [ { "resourceType": "third-party", "budget": 0 } ] }, { "path": "/publications/*", "resourceSizes": [ { "resourceType": "total", "budget": 250 }, { "resourceType": "image", "budget": 140 } ] } ] ``` `third-party: 0` is the real guard rail. Run `lhci autorun --budgetPath=budget.json` on every PR. --- ## 2. Accessibility — WCAG 2.2 AA ### Correct conformance levels (verified against the normative W3C spec — most blog posts get 2.4.12 and 3.3.7 wrong) | SC | Name | Level | |---|---|---| | 2.4.11 | Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | **AA** | | 2.4.12 | Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | AAA | | 2.4.13 | Focus Appearance | AAA | | 2.5.7 | Dragging Movements | **AA** | | 2.5.8 | Target Size (Minimum) — **24×24 CSS px** | **AA** | | 3.2.6 | Consistent Help | A | | 3.3.7 | Redundant Entry | A | | 3.3.8 | Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | **AA** | Contrast, quoted: 1.4.3 — *"a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except… Large Text [with] at least 18 point or 14 point bold… at least 3:1"*. 1.4.11 — *"at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s)"* for UI Components and Graphical Objects. ### Colour — the one that always fails The academic-site signature bug is grey metadata. On white: | Colour | Ratio | Verdict | |---|---|---| | `#999999` | 2.85:1 | **FAIL** | | `#8A8A8A` | 3.54:1 | fails body, passes large only | | `#767676` | 4.54:1 | minimum pass for body | | `#6B6B6B` | 5.30:1 | comfortable | | `#595959` | 7.00:1 | use this for "muted" | In dark mode, avoid pure `#FFF` on pure `#000` — the halation makes serif text shimmer. Use ~`#E8E6E3` on ~`#16181A` (≈14:1). ### Focus — and WCAG 2.2's new trap ```css :where(a,button,input,select,textarea,summary,[tabindex]):focus-visible{ outline:2px solid var(--focus); /* ≥3:1 vs BOTH the component and the page */ outline-offset:2px; border-radius:2px; } :where(a,button):focus:not(:focus-visible){ outline:none; } @supports not selector(:focus-visible){ :where(a,button):focus{ outline:2px solid var(--focus); outline-offset:2px; } } ``` **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (AA)** is the new one that bites: a sticky header hides the focused element when tabbing backwards. Either don't use a sticky header, or: ```css :root{ --header-h: 4rem; } [id]{ scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--header-h) + 1rem); } ``` **2.5.8 Target Size (AA, 24×24)** bites on: tag/filter chips, the social-icon row, pagination, the theme toggle, and the tiny year links in a publication list. ```css .icon-btn, .tag-chip, .pagination a{ min-block-size:44px; min-inline-size:44px; display:inline-grid; place-items:center; } /* 44 = 2.5.5 AAA / Apple HIG */ ``` ### Skip link ```html Skip to content …
``` ```css .skip-link{ position:absolute; left:-9999px; } .skip-link:focus{ left:1rem; top:1rem; position:fixed; z-index:100; background:var(--bg); color:var(--fg); padding:.75rem 1rem; outline:2px solid var(--focus); outline-offset:2px; } ``` ### Heading order — this is how blind readers actually navigate WebAIM Screen Reader Survey #10: **71.6% navigate a long page by headings first** (78% of advanced users) vs 13.6% find-in-page, 4.8% links, **3.7% landmarks**. 88.8% rate heading levels useful. Landmarks are nice but headings are the load-bearing structure. - Exactly one `

A publications page with 40 links called "PDF" is a screen-reader link-list of 40 identical entries. ```html PDF — Regonda et al. 2024, Urban flood forecasting for Hyderabad ``` ```css .vh{ position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; overflow:hidden; clip-path:inset(50%); white-space:nowrap; } ``` Use a visually-hidden span or `aria-label` — **never `title=`** (not surfaced to most AT, not shown on touch, not keyboard-reachable). ### Alt text for scientific figures W3C WAI complex-images guidance, quoted: the text alternative has two parts — *"The first part is the short description to identify the image and, where appropriate, indicate the location of the long description. The second part is the long description – a textual representation of the essential information conveyed by the image."* Their model chart alt: *"Bar chart showing monthly and total visitors for the first quarter 2025 for sites 1 to 3."* **House rule for this site — three layers:** 1. **`alt` = what it IS.** Chart type + variables + place + period. ≤ ~125 chars. exemplars.name: Jon Barron, Google DeepMind
exemplars.what_works: A single-page site with no nav chrome at all: bio, contact links, headshot, then everything else is publications. Papers are grouped by section (main papers, micropapers, recorded talks, service) and reverse-chronological within each. Every entry carries a thumbnail, title linked to the project page or arXiv, a co-author list with each name hyperlinked, venue + year, an inline award badge, up to four resource links (project / arXiv / video / code) and a one-to-two-sentence plain-language description. Plain HTML, system serif, information density over whitespace. Zero framework.
exemplars.steal_this: The per-paper metadata row: thumbnail + title + linked co-authors + venue/year + award badge + up to four consistently-ordered resource links + a one-sentence plain-language gloss. Encode exactly those as columns in the Google Sheet and the publication list writes itself — and the one-sentence gloss is the thing that makes a publications page readable by a journalist, a prospective student, or a funding officer rather than only by peers.

exemplars.name: Karl Broman, University of Wisconsin–Madison
exemplars.what_works: Flat horizontal nav across about / publications / talks / software / teaching / tutorials, with secondary links to CV, GitHub and Mastodon. The homepage leads with four publication FIGURES as visual entry points rather than a wall of citations, each linking through to detail — research output presented visually before it is presented bibliographically. Radical minimalism: no hero, no carousel, no imagery except the science itself.
exemplars.steal_this: Lead the homepage with 3-4 real research figures (a hydrograph, an inundation map, a forecast skill plot) as the primary visual identity, each a link into the work. For a hydrologist this is both more distinctive and more honest than a stock photo of water, and it costs ~40 KB if the figures ship as SVG.

exemplars.name: Gwern Branwen, independent researcher
exemplars.what_works: The most rigorous longevity and dark-mode engineering on the public web. Stated principles: 'local > remote—every link dies someday' and 'archives are expensive short-term but cheap long-term'. Preemptive local archiving of every external URL with ArchiveBox, plus link checking in three phases (writing time, compilation, post-deployment), with [ARCHIVE] fallbacks offered alongside originals. Dark mode uses per-image ML classification via InvertOrNot.com rather than blanket inversion. Fonts are subsetted; 'JavaScript is not required for the core reading experience'; math compiles to native HTML+CSS+Unicode ('√4', '1⁄2') where possible instead of a JS renderer. Monochrome grayscale palette so no information is carried by colour alone. Pages remain readable in elinks.
exemplars.steal_this: Two things. (1) The three-phase link check plus preemptive archiving, and the [archived] companion link pattern — this is the only serious answer to link rot on a site whose value is its citations. (2) Per-image inversion decided at build time by InvertOrNot, never a global CSS filter.

exemplars.name: Bartosz Ciechanowski, independent
exemplars.what_works: The reference standard for explaining physical processes on the web. Clean semantic heading structure. Interactive figures built with Canvas/WebGL, but with disciplined accessibility: information is encoded redundantly in colour AND shape/position ('red point is the descending node, green point is the ascending node'), every demonstration is accompanied by prose that carries the same meaning, and controls include toggles between realistic and exaggerated proportions for legibility. Progressive complexity — simple two-body systems before 1200-particle ones.
exemplars.steal_this: The redundant-encoding discipline: never let colour alone carry meaning in a figure, and always write the prose so the figure is an illustration rather than the sole carrier of the point. Directly transferable to hydrographs (dash pattern + marker as well as colour for each series) and to inundation maps (the caption names the spatial pattern in words).

exemplars.name: Dan Luu, independent
exemplars.what_works: Hard measured evidence for the performance budget. His ~0.01-0.1 MB text site loads in 1.6 s on dial-up and 6.4 s on a deliberately hostile link (dial-up bandwidth, 1000 ms ping, 10% packet loss). Google.com (0.59 MB) takes 94 s on dial-up and 6.8 s on 3G; amazon.com (4.4 MB) takes 265 s and 36 s; joelonsoftware.com times out entirely after six minutes. His own site got a 20x speedup mostly by moving script includes to the footer.
exemplars.steal_this: The argument, and the numbers, for defending a 175 KB budget against every future 'can we just add this widget' request. Also the underlying design stance: near-pure semantic HTML with minimal CSS is not an aesthetic limitation, it is what makes a site work on the connections a large share of Indian readers actually have.

exemplars.name: arXiv, Cornell University
exemplars.what_works: Verified by raw curl: a minimal, correct Highwire Press implementation — citation_title, repeated citation_author in 'Surname, Given' form, citation_date as 2023/11/18, citation_online_date, citation_pdf_url pointing at the full text, and citation_abstract. Its robots.txt Allows /abs, /pdf, /list and /html while Disallowing /user, /e-print, /src — exactly the shape Scholar asks for (open the articles and the browse pages, close the dynamically generated spaces).
exemplars.steal_this: The minimum viable tag set, proven in production on the most-crawled preprint server in the world: title, one tag per author, date, pdf_url, abstract. Copy the field names and the date format literally. Also copy the robots.txt posture: allow everything that is a paper or leads to one.

exemplars.name: Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (Copernicus / EGU)
exemplars.what_works: Verified by raw curl: the complete journal-grade Highwire set in his own field — citation_publisher, citation_journal_title, citation_publication_date (2024/01/02), citation_volume, citation_issue, citation_issn, citation_doi, citation_firstpage, citation_lastpage, plus citation_author_institution and citation_author_orcid interleaved after each citation_author, and citation_fulltext_world_readable to signal open access. The abstract is in the page, in full, with no interaction required.
exemplars.steal_this: The exact field list and interleaving order for a hydrology journal paper — including citation_author_orcid, which most personal sites omit and which materially helps author disambiguation for a name with variants (Satish Regonda / Satish Kumar Regonda / S. K. Regonda). Use this page as the ground-truth template for the publication page's <head>.

exemplars.name: Satish Kumar Regonda, IIT Hyderabad (existing faculty page)
exemplars.what_works: The authoritative institutional record. Confirms: Associate Professor, Civil Engineering AND Climate Change, satishr@ce.iith.ac.in, research interests listed as 'Urban and Rural Flood Modeling, Climate Sciences, Data Sciences, Statistical Modeling Techniques, Ensemble Forecasting, Multiscale Modelling, AI/ML, Climate Change'. It lists a Google Sites homepage but NO ORCID and NO Google Scholar link. It also uses the name form 'Satish Kumar Regonda' where the Google Site uses 'Satish Regonda'.
exemplars.steal_this: Two actions rather than a design pattern. (1) The IITH page is a high-authority inbound link and it currently points at the Google Site — get it updated to satishregonda.in on launch day; that single edit does more for the name query than any on-page SEO. (2) The IITH keyword string is his own self-description; mine it for knowsAbout in the JSON-LD and for the site's actual section names, so the vocabulary on the new site matches the vocabulary Google already associates with him.

pitfalls: Hiding publication abstracts behind an accordion or 'read more' toggle. Scholar states outright that the site must not require users or robots to 'click on links or buttons, or scroll down the page before they can read the entire abstract' — a design flourish that silently removes him from Google Scholar, with no error message and a 6-9 month correction latency.

Fetching the Google Sheet client-side at runtime. Scholar's crawler does not execute JS ('the use of Flash, JavaScript, or form-based navigation makes it hard for our automated system to find your articles'), the publications would be invisible to Google, the JS budget would be blown, and the site would break permanently the day the Sheet is deleted. It must be build-time with the data committed to the repo.

Putting PDFs in a central /pdfs/ or /assets/ folder. citation_pdf_url 'must refer to a file in the same subdirectory as the HTML abstract' — a tidy-looking asset layout silently breaks Scholar's ability to associate the PDF with its metadata, and the PDF then gets indexed as a separate, metadata-free document.

Global filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg) for dark mode. It turns his headshot into a negative and reverses the meaning of every diverging colormap — a red-means-anomalously-wet map now says the opposite of the paper. Inversion must be per-image, build-time-classified, and restricted to black-on-white line art.

Trusting MDN's font-display page, which states 'swap is generally best for CLS'. It is the worst: an infinite swap period guarantees a reflow whenever the font arrives late. Only `optional` (100 ms block, 0 ms swap) is CLS-safe.
Light grey metadata. #999 on white is 2.85:1 and fails 1.4.3 outright. Every academic template does this to journal names, years and author lists — precisely the text a reader most needs to scan.

A dark-mode site with no print reset. Browsers do not print background colours but do print text colours, so a dark theme prints as faint grey (or invisible) text on white. Nobody discovers this until a search committee prints his CV.

Forty links labelled 'PDF' on the publications page. #3 on WebAIM's screen-reader problem list, a Level A failure of 2.4.4, and it makes the link rotor useless on exactly the page where a screen-reader user is most likely to be scanning.

Using Google Fonts CDN 'because it's cached'. Browser HTTP cache has been partitioned per-site for years, so there is no cross-site cache benefit left — only a render-blocking third-origin stylesheet costing ~3 extra RTTs (≈450 ms at India's typical RTT) and an IP transfer to a third country that turns a zero-data site into one with a DPDP notice obligation.

Embedding YouTube, Twitter or Google Maps iframes. Each sets third-party cookies before any interaction, adds hundreds of KB, tanks INP, and converts 'we collect nothing' into a consent problem. Use a click-to-load facade or a plain outbound link.

Expanding link URLs in print across the whole page (a[href^="http"]::after) rather than only in prose. On a publications page where every title, DOI and PDF is a link, the printout becomes an unreadable thicket of URLs.

Date-based blog URLs (/2026/09/04/slug/). He will backdate posts, misremember dates, and want to revise older notes — and every one of those becomes a permanent redirect. /notes/<slug>/ has none of these failure modes.

Slugs derived from Sheet row IDs or row order. The moment he re-sorts the spreadsheet, every publication URL changes and every external citation of those URLs breaks. Slugs must be derived from stable content (year + short title) and frozen on first publish.

Shipping a client-side-filtered publications list with no server-rendered fallback. It fails for Scholar, fails for Google, fails with JS disabled, fails on a flaky 3G connection where the JS request times out, and fails keyboard/screen-reader users unless the filter widgets are real form controls.

Assuming Person or ScholarlyArticle JSON-LD will produce a rich result. Neither is in Google's supported rich-results gallery. ProfilePage is. Mark up ScholarlyArticle for correctness, but do not let anyone claim it as the SEO strategy — the Highwire meta tags are the mechanism that actually reaches Scholar.

Leaving the old Google Site live and fully populated. It will compete with satishregonda.in for his own name, and Google Sites permits neither a 301 nor a custom canonical tag, so the only remedy is to strip it to a one-line pointer.

Relying on KaTeX or MathJax for a handful of equations — hundreds of KB, font-swap CLS, a hard JS dependency, and colours that need manual dark-mode handling, when MathML Core has been Baseline since January 2023 and inherits currentColor for free.

Icon-only social links and filter chips sized to the glyph. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires 24×24 CSS px minimum; a 16px icon with 4px padding fails, and the failure is invisible in every desktop screenshot.

Publishing his email as 'satishr.at.iith.ac.in' or as an image. Screen readers read the first literally, the second not at all, and neither can be copy-pasted — while the address sits in plain text on the IITH faculty page anyway, so the obfuscation protects nothing and costs everything.

Blur-up LQIP placeholders on a text-heavy site. Each costs 300-600 bytes inline plus a decode, on a page where the reader is looking at prose. A flat average-colour background costs ~20 bytes and prevents exactly the same CLS.
